newsitem.title: USA: Store's hot tub display sickened nearby customers.
newsitem.headline: Store's hot tub display sickened nearby customers.

text.p: Federal health officials said Thursday they may issue new maintenance guidelines for whirlpool spas after a contaminated hot tub on display in a home-improvement store in Christiansburg, Virginia, caused two people to die from Legionnaires Disease last fall.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said 22 people who were hospitalized with Legionnaires disease in October had stood near the contaminated whirlpool spa, without ever getting in the water. Two of the patients died.

"There have been whirlpool spa outbreaks, but never have we observed an outbreak where all of the people exposed were outside of the spa itself. They weren't actually using it. They were just standing around it or perhaps even walking by," CDC epidemiologist Dr. Robert Breiman said.
The CDC, which last year issued guidelines to minimize transmission of Legionnaires disease from whirlpool spas on cruise ships, said similar recommendations may be needed for land-based spas.
Many of those who became ill said they had spent more than an hour in the store. One man said he stood near the hot tub display for almost a half an hour while waiting for a salesperson to help him.
"Mists or aerosols from this operating whirlpool spa that was on display were contaminated with Legionella and exposed people who were in the area of the store around the display," Breiman said.
The contaminated hot tub at the home store had been taken out of service by the time the most of the illnesses developed. Bacteria had contaminated the spa's filter.
Legionella bacteria, which can be carried in aerosol droplets, has also been found in air-conditioning cooling towers, showers, fountains, humidifiers and respiratory therapy equipment.
The organisms are common and usually do not cause disease, but in some cases they cause pneumonia.

The disease got its name after an outbreak occurred among a group of persons attending an American Legion convention in Philadelphia in 1976. It usually affects men over 50 years of age, especially those who have underlying medical problems.
